hints: Identify the longest carbon chain that includes the aldehyde carbon, remembering the CHO carbon is always C1.
walkthrough:
Find the parent chain including the aldehyde**
You are looking at $(CH_3)_3CCHO$. Count the CHO carbon as C1. The longest chain through it is 3 carbons, so the parent is propanal. The C2 carbon carries two methyl groups, so add 2,2-dimethyl in front.
Final answer: 2,2-dimethylpropanal

hints: Look at the starred carbon in C*=O, count its sigma bonded regions and recall the shape of a carbonyl carbon.
walkthrough:
Count regions around the carbonyl carbon**
The starred carbon joins to one alkyl group, one H and double bonds to O. That is three sigma regions in a trigonal planar arrangement with one p orbital left for the pi bond. Three regions means $\text{sp}^2$ hybridisation.

hints: Recall which strong oxidising agent converts an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid and whether heating should be gentle reflux or distillation here.
walkthrough:
Link aldehyde to acid conversion**
Reaction 1 turns $(CH_3)_3CCHO$ into $(CH_3)_3CCO_2H$. Only a strong oxidiser will do this fully. Use acidified potassium dichromate(VI) with heating under reflux so the aldehyde is not lost by distillation before oxidation is complete.
Final answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, heat under reflux

hints: Compare the functional groups in A, a carboxylic acid, and B, an ester, and decide which one has an O-H bond able to hydrogen bond.
Identify the strongest intermolecular force available to the ester B which has no O-H or N-H bond.
Relate the relative strength of these forces to the energy needed to separate particles to melt the solid.
walkthrough:
Spot the hydrogen bonding in A**
A is $(CH_3)_3CCO_2H$, a carboxylic acid with an $O-H$ group attached to a very electronegative O. Molecules of A can hydrogen bond to each other, even forming dimers. This is a very strong intermolecular attraction.

See what B cannot do**
B is $CH_3CO_2(CH_2)_2CH_3$, an ester. It has polar $C=O$ and $C-O$ bonds so it has permanent dipole-dipole forces plus London dispersion forces, but with no $O-H$ it cannot hydrogen bond to itself.

Connect strength to physical state**
Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than ordinary dipole-dipole forces. Far more thermal energy is needed to break the network in A to allow melting, so A stays solid at room temperature while B with weaker forces is already liquid.

Final answer: A has hydrogen bonding between molecules.
B has only permanent dipole-dipole / van der Waals forces between molecules.
Hydrogen bonding is stronger and needs more energy to overcome, so A is solid while B is liquid.

hints: Remember NaBH4 acts as a source of hydrogen atoms for reduction and the aldehyde CHO becomes CH2OH.
walkthrough:
Write reduction with [H]**
$NaBH_4$ reduces the aldehyde to a primary alcohol S, $(CH_3)_3CCH_2OH$. Using $[H]$ to show reducing hydrogen, the balanced equation is $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCHO} + 2\text{[H]} \rightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CCH}_2\text{OH}$.

hints: Look at ester U and split it at the COO group to see which acid part came from A and which alkyl part came from T.
Recall the catalyst normally added for esterification of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from the ester U**
U is $(CH_3)_3CCOOCH(CH_3)_2$. The left side $(CH_3)_3CCO$ comes from acid A. The right side $OCH(CH_3)_2$ must come from the alcohol T. So T is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, propan-2-ol.

Add the esterification catalyst**
Reaction 2 is esterification, a reversible condensation. A few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, catalyse it and help remove water.

Final answer: T is propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$
Catalyst: concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / sulfuric acid

hints: Recall what a positive 2,4-DNPH result looks like for any aldehyde or ketone.
walkthrough:
Apply the carbonyl test**
Both X and Y contain $C=O$ and so both give a positive 2,4-DNPH test. The expected observation is an orange, yellow or red precipitate of the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone.
Final answer: Orange / yellow / red precipitate for both X and Y

hints: Remember which type of carbonyl is oxidised by Fehling's solution to give a red precipitate and which is not.
walkthrough:
Distinguish aldehyde from ketone**
Y gives a red precipitate with Fehling's solution while X does not. Only aldehydes reduce Fehling's solution, so Y must contain the aldehyde group. X must be the ketone.
Final answer: Aldehyde

hints: Think about how many different groups must be attached to a single carbon for it to be chiral.
walkthrough:
Define the chiral centre**
A chiral centre is a carbon atom attached to four different atoms or groups of atoms, so its mirror image is non-superimposable.
Final answer: A carbon atom bonded to four different atoms / groups

hints: Deduce the structure of Y as the only chiral aldehyde isomer of C5H10O, with chiral carbon bonded to CHO, H, CH3 and C2H5.
Recall how to draw a pair of enantiomers using solid wedge and hashed wedge bonds that are mirror images.
walkthrough:
Identify Y**
Y is an aldehyde isomer of $(CH_3)_3CCHO$, formula $C_5H_{10}O$, that is chiral. This is 2-methylbutanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$. The chiral carbon is C2, bonded to $H$, $CH_3$, $C_2H_5$ and $CHO$.

Draw non-superimposable mirrors**
Draw the chiral C tetrahedrally with two bonds in the plane, one solid wedge coming out and one hashed wedge going back. Then draw the second isomer as the mirror image with wedge and dash exchanged, keeping the same four groups. The two structures must be mirror images that cannot be superimposed.

Final answer: Y is 2-methylbutanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3\text{)CHO}$. Pair of enantiomers with tetrahedral chiral C bonded to $\text{CHO}$, $\text{H}$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$ drawn in 3D with wedge / dash swapped.

hints: Match each wavenumber range to its characteristic bond using the Data Booklet: broad O-H, C=C and C-O.
walkthrough:
Assign the three peaks**
The broad absorption at $3200-3600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the $O-H$ stretch of an alcohol, $1630 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the $C=C$ stretch of an alkene, and $1050 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ is the $C-O$ stretch. Together they point to an unsaturated alcohol for Z.
Final answer: $3200-3600 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ : $\text{O-H}$ / $\text{RO-H}$ ; $1630 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ : $\text{C=C}$ ; $1050 \text{ cm}^{-1}$ : $\text{C-O}$

hints: Use the IR evidence to confirm Z contains both C=C and an alcohol OH on a C5 skeleton.
Remember geometrical isomerism needs each C of the double bond to carry two different groups.
Ensure the chain is branched, for example with a methyl side chain, while still allowing E/Z isomerism.
walkthrough:
Build a C5 alkene alcohol**
Z has formula $C_5H_{10}O$ with one $C=C$ and one $OH$, so draw a five carbon skeletal chain containing a double bond and a $CH_2OH$ or $CHOH$ group.

Make it branched and able to show E/Z**
A straight chain like pent-2-en-1-ol would show geometrical isomerism but is not branched. Add a methyl branch while keeping two different groups on each alkene carbon, for example $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$. Here the left $C$ has $CH_3$ and $H$, the right $C$ has $CH_3$ and $CH_2OH$, so cis-trans isomers exist.

Draw as skeletal**
In skeletal form show zigzag lines for carbons, a double line for $C=C$ and an $OH$ on the end carbon, with the methyl branch clearly shown.
Final answer: Skeletal formula of a branched C5 alkenol showing E/Z isomerism, e.g. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{OH}$ (2-methylbut-2-en-1-ol, either E or Z form)

hints: Deduce the structure of ketone X from the product (C2H5)2C(OH)CN as pentan-3-one and show the polar C=O dipole.
Start with attack of CN- on the delta positive carbonyl carbon and movement of the C=O pi bond onto oxygen.
Finish by showing protonation of the alkoxide intermediate by HCN or H+ to give the hydroxynitrile.
walkthrough:
Draw X with its dipole**
X must be pentan-3-one, $\text{(C}_2\text{H}_5\text{)}_2\text{C=O}$, because addition of $HCN$ gives $(C_2H_5)_2C(OH)CN$. Show the carbonyl polarised as $C^{\delta+}$ and $O^{\delta-}$ because oxygen pulls the pi electrons towards itself.

Nucleophilic attack to form the intermediate**
Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ to the $C^{\delta+}$ atom, and a second curly arrow from the $C=O$ double bond onto the O. This forms a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, $(C_2H_5)_2C(CN)O^{-}$, with the negative charge on oxygen.

Protonate to give the hydroxynitrile**
Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on the $O^{-}$ to an $H^{+}$ from $HCN$. This gives the final product $(C_2H_5)_2C(OH)CN$ and regenerates $CN^{-}$. Include all lone pairs, charges and arrows carefully.

Final answer: X is $\text{(C}_2\text{H}_5\text{)}_2\text{C=O}$ with $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{O}^{\delta-}$ shown. $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks $\text{C=O}$ carbon, $\text{C=O}$ bond breaks to $\text{O}^{-}$ to give $\text{(C}_2\text{H}_5\text{)}_2\text{C(CN)O}^{-}$ intermediate, then protonated to product.

hints: Consider whether NaCN is used up in the HCN addition or regenerated at the end.
walkthrough:
Spot the regenerated species**
$CN^{-}$ from $NaCN$ attacks first but is regenerated when the intermediate takes $H^{+}$ from $HCN$. Because it speeds up the reaction without being consumed, $NaCN$ acts as a catalyst.
Final answer: Catalyst
